title: Senior Living Research Digest — New This Week — 2026-10-05
secondary_audience: families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

studies.title: Behavioral sleep programs help dementia caregivers rest — but the evidence is thinner than it looks
studies.the_study: Researchers searched eleven databases and pooled 21 randomized controlled trials covering 1,964 unpaid family caregivers of people with mild cognitive impairment or dementia (average age 64, about three-quarters women) to test whether non-drug approaches — behavioral sleep training, psychoeducation, and similar programs — improve sleep. Across the five trials (334 caregivers) that could be combined statistically, these programs cut scores on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index by an average of 1.27 points compared with usual care or attention control. However, every trial carried a high overall risk of bias and the authors rated the certainty of the evidence as very low.
studies.why_it_matters: Caregivers of people with dementia are chronically sleep-deprived, and poor caregiver sleep is tied to depression, health decline, and earlier nursing home placement for the person being cared for — so even modest, drug-free gains matter, especially as sleeping pills carry real risks in this age group.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are caring for a spouse or partner with dementia and your own sleep has collapsed, know that structured behavioral and educational programs have been tested in randomized trials and show modest benefit — worth asking your doctor, local Area Agency on Aging, or Alzheimer's Association chapter what sleep-focused caregiver programs are available near you before reaching for a sleep medication.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living operators and dementia care programs: this review is a reminder that the caregiver's sleep is a measurable, modifiable outcome — but also that the trial evidence is weak enough that organizations adopting a sleep curriculum should track results locally rather than assume effectiveness.
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of the primary outcome rested on just five trials with 334 participants total; all included trials had high risk of bias and the evidence was graded very low certainty; sleep quality was self-reported via questionnaire rather than objectively measured; effect size was small and durability beyond end-of-intervention was not established.

studies.title: Volunteering and video calls ease loneliness in older adults — scrolling social media does the opposite
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed two waves of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (N=7,547 in 2023, mean age 75; N=6,543 in 2024, mean age 76), comparing nine kinds of social participation against self-reported loneliness. Working and volunteering were tied to lower loneliness at baseline, while visiting social networking sites was tied to higher loneliness. Over the two years, continued volunteering and newly starting video calls with family or friends predicted lower loneliness, even after accounting for prior loneliness. Notably, in-person visits, outings for enjoyment, caregiving, religious services and club meetings showed no significant association.
studies.why_it_matters: The default advice to lonely older adults — get out more, see people — may be less effective than structured, purposeful activity such as volunteering, and the finding that a greater number of different activities tracked with less loneliness gives families and programs a concrete target.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you feel lonely, consider whether your social time has a purpose attached to it: in this large national study, older adults who kept volunteering, who worked, and who newly took up video calls with family reported less loneliness two years later, while time spent on social networking sites went the other way. You might experiment with swapping some scrolling for a standing video call or a volunteer shift and see how it feels.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living operators and activity directors, this is a nudge to audit the calendar: club meetings, group outings and religious services — the staples of most activity programs — showed no measurable loneliness benefit here, while volunteering opportunities and help setting up video calls did. Building genuine volunteer roles for residents, inside or outside the community, may be a better use of staff time than adding another social event.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish causation, and lonelier people may gravitate to social media rather than the reverse. Loneliness and participation were self-reported; follow-up was only two years.

studies.title: Not all loneliness is the same — and the existential kind hits older adults hardest
studies.the_study: Turkish researchers surveyed 237 adults aged 65 and older (mean age 70.9) and separated loneliness into three types: social (lacking a wider network), emotional (lacking close bonds), and existential (a deeper sense of separateness and questioning of meaning). All three types were associated with depressive symptoms, but existential loneliness showed the strongest link — and it was the only type significantly associated with anxiety.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that filling an older person's calendar with company may not touch the kind of loneliness most closely tied to their distress, and that conversations about meaning, mortality and purpose deserve a place in late-life mental health care.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have plenty of people around you and still feel profoundly alone, that experience has a name — existential loneliness — and in this study it was the form most strongly linked to both low mood and anxiety. It may be worth raising directly with your doctor or a counselor rather than assuming more social contact is the answer.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care staff, the takeaway is that visits and group activities address only part of the picture. Making room for conversations about meaning, legacy and loss — rather than steering away from them — may matter more for a resident's mood than another activity sign-up.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational, so direction of effect is unknown; modest sample (N=237) from a single country; all measures self-reported; findings from a Turkish sample may not generalize elsewhere.

studies.title: When grown children fall short of expectations, older parents pay a mental health price
studies.the_study: Reviewing 15 years of published research (2011-2025) across six databases, with quality appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute tools, researchers examined 'filial discrepancy' — the gap between the care and support older parents expect from adult children and what they actually receive. Across studies, larger gaps were consistently associated with late-life depressive symptoms and loneliness. A recurring finding: the emotional quality of the parent-child relationship mattered more than how physically close children lived.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes a common source of family guilt — distance — as less important than the warmth and reciprocity of the relationship itself, which is something families can actually work on.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you find yourself quietly disappointed in how much your children are present for you, know that this gap between expectation and reality is a recognized risk factor for depression and loneliness — and that naming expectations out loud, rather than waiting for them to be met, is where researchers see the relationship quality that protects mood.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For adult children and care professionals, especially those working with families from Confucian or other strongly filial cultural traditions, this is a reminder that moving a parent closer or increasing visit frequency may not resolve distress if the parent perceives the support as inadequate or obligatory. Asking directly what a parent expected, and what feels missing, may be more useful than logistics.
studies.caveats: Narrative review of heterogeneous observational studies — no pooled effect size and no causal inference possible. Evidence is concentrated in Confucian cultural contexts and may not generalize to Western family structures.

studies.title: Phone calls and visits from adult children eased depression in older Icelanders over five years
studies.the_study: Researchers followed participants in the Age, Gene/Environment Susceptibility–Reykjavik Study (AGES-Reykjavik) across two waves — 5,764 community-dwelling older adults at baseline (2002–2006) and 3,316 at follow-up (2007–2011), with mean ages of 77 and 78 — tracking seven measures of social contact alongside Geriatric Depression Scale scores. Among those with few depressive symptoms, meeting with children or friends and feeling close to family or friends predicted lower depression scores five years later. Among those already scoring high on depressive symptoms, the biggest reductions came from telephoning children and meeting with children — telephone contact with children was associated with a GDS drop of nearly five points.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that for older adults who are already struggling with low mood, regular contact with adult children — including something as simple as a phone call — tracks with meaningful improvement years later, while for those doing well, friendships matter just as much as family.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your mood has been low, the kind of contact that mattered most in this study wasn't a big gathering — it was ordinary, repeated contact with your children, including by phone. Consider telling your family that regular calls are something you actually want, and ask your doctor whether a check on your social connections belongs in your routine visits alongside blood pressure and medications.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care staff: this is a case for scheduling, not spontaneity. The study points to routine phone contact with adult children as the strongest correlate of improvement among residents with higher depression scores — a cue for senior living staff to build calling time into the week and to flag residents whose phone and visit logs have gone quiet.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish causation, and low mood may itself reduce social contact (reverse causation is plausible). Depressive symptoms were measured by screening scale, not clinical diagnosis. Substantial attrition between waves (5,764 to 3,316). Single-country Icelandic population may not generalize to more dispersed or culturally different families.

studies.title: A step-counter and a simple self-monitoring routine broke up long sitting spells in older day-care clients with heart conditions
studies.the_study: This was an exploratory secondary analysis of a Japanese randomized controlled trial run at a daycare center from October 2022 to January 2023. Of 52 older adults receiving long-term care in the parent trial, 36 had cardiovascular conditions and 33 had usable data (19 intervention, 14 control). Those given an accelerometer and guided to self-monitor their activity showed significant changes versus controls in daily step count, sedentary time accumulated in bouts of 1 minute or more and 30 minutes or more, number of sedentary bouts, and light physical activity — but no change in moderate-to-vigorous activity or quality-of-life scores.
studies.why_it_matters: Prolonged uninterrupted sitting is an independent cardiovascular risk, and this suggests the fix for frail older adults in long-term care may not be formal exercise at all, but simply seeing your own numbers and standing up more often.
studies.story_angle_primary: If vigorous exercise isn't realistic for you, this small trial suggests a different target: interrupting long stretches of sitting. Wearing a step counter and actually checking it was linked to more light movement and fewer 30-minute sitting spells — ask your physiotherapist or day program whether they can set you up with a device and a daily number to watch.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For day centers and long-term care operators: the measurable gains here were in light activity and sit-to-stand breaks, not workout intensity — a reminder that programming and staffing aimed at frequent small interruptions may be more achievable, and more measurable, than exercise classes most residents can't sustain.
studies.caveats: Small N (33 analyzed) and an exploratory secondary analysis of a trial not designed or powered for this question — the authors explicitly call it hypothesis-generating. Single center, short duration (roughly four months of recruitment window), no change in quality of life, and no evidence yet of any clinical cardiovascular benefit. Japanese long-term care daycare population may not generalize.

studies.title: Adding a second drug to donepezil hasn't yet been proven better than donepezil alone for Alzheimer's
studies.the_study: Researchers pooled 41 randomized controlled trials covering 9,822 people with Alzheimer's disease to compare donepezil (Aricept) alone against donepezil combined with a second agent — including memantine, masitinib, DL-3-n-butylphthalide and a traditional Chinese medicine capsule. Several combinations beat placebo on cognition (MMSE, ADAS-cog) and on daily-living ability (ADCS-ADL), with donepezil plus masitinib ranking highest. But when compared head-to-head with donepezil by itself, no combination reached statistical significance on any outcome; the trends simply pointed in a favorable direction. The authors rated the certainty of the evidence as mostly moderate to low.
studies.why_it_matters: Many families are told that layering a second medication onto a cholinesterase inhibitor will slow decline further; this pooled analysis shows the evidence for that extra benefit is still suggestive rather than proven, which matters when weighing cost, pill burden and side effects.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your doctor proposes adding a second Alzheimer's medication to donepezil, it's reasonable to ask what measurable benefit is expected, how it will be tracked, and when you'd stop if nothing changes — the pooled trial evidence so far shows trends, not proof of added benefit over donepezil alone.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care staff and family decision-makers: this is a useful reference point when a resident is on multiple cognition drugs. It supports periodic medication review and realistic expectation-setting with families, rather than assuming more drugs equals more protection.
studies.caveats: Network meta-analysis of published trials, not new patient data; certainty of evidence rated mostly moderate to low; many included trials were short; some comparator drugs (masitinib, DL-3-n-butylphthalide, Dengzhan shengmai capsule) are not widely available or approved in the US; indirect comparisons can be unreliable.

studies.title: One in three cerebral stroke-clot survivors has lasting cognitive problems — even those who look fully recovered
studies.the_study: A systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 11 observational studies and one randomized trial covering 801 people who had survived cerebral venous thrombosis — a clot in the brain's draining veins — with at least six months of follow-up. Cognitive impairment was found in 19% to 29% of survivors overall, with memory affected in roughly 39% and executive/visuospatial function in about 36%. Strikingly, even among patients rated as having no functional disability at all on the modified Rankin Scale, 28.6% had measurable cognitive impairment.
studies.why_it_matters: The standard yardstick for stroke recovery — whether someone can walk and manage daily tasks — misses thinking, memory and planning problems in roughly a third of survivors, meaning many people are discharged as 'fully recovered' while still struggling.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or someone close to you has had any kind of stroke and been told the recovery is complete because walking and daily function returned, it's worth asking for a formal cognitive assessment — memory and executive-function problems can persist invisibly behind a clean physical bill of health.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and rehabilitation staff: a discharge score of 'no disability' should not end the conversation. Watch for difficulty with planning, multitasking, finances and new learning in the months after discharge, and push for cognitive screening in follow-up visits rather than waiting for a crisis.
studies.caveats: Observational studies predominate (cannot establish causation); cerebral venous thrombosis mainly affects younger adults, particularly women, so findings may not generalize to typical older stroke populations; very wide confidence intervals and high heterogeneity across studies; cognitive testing methods varied between studies.

studies.title: Vitamin E for brain blood flow: decades of research, and not a single human trial
studies.the_study: Australian researchers searched six databases for any study testing whether vitamin E affects cerebrovascular function — the brain's blood flow and vessel responsiveness, which declines with normal aging. Of 335 records, they found zero clinical studies in humans. The only evidence came from 10 preclinical animal studies, where vitamin E improved cerebral blood flow, reduced intracranial pressure and delayed clot formation in models of stroke and reduced brain perfusion.
studies.why_it_matters: Vitamin E is widely marketed and taken by older adults for 'brain health,' yet this review documents that the specific claim about brain blood flow rests entirely on animal data, with no human trial ever conducted.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're taking a vitamin E supplement hoping to protect brain circulation as you age, know that no human study has ever tested that — and because vitamin E affects platelet clumping, it's worth telling your doctor or pharmacist you take it, especially if you're also on a blood thinner or aspirin.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For caregivers and senior living staff managing residents' supplement lists: this review is a reminder that over-the-counter vitamin E has no clinical evidence base for cerebrovascular benefit, and belongs in the medication reconciliation conversation because of its anti-platelet effects.
studies.caveats: Systematic review with no human studies to analyze; preclinical animal findings often fail to translate; heterogeneous study designs prevented meta-analysis; conclusions about human benefit or harm cannot be drawn from this evidence.

studies.title: Insurance gets you the blood test — but it doesn't close the diabetes care gap
studies.the_study: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 12 US studies published between 2000 and 2025 examining how insurance status (private, Medicare, Medicaid, or uninsured) relates to the quality of type 2 diabetes care. Having insurance was significantly associated with greater odds of receiving HbA1c testing, but showed no statistically significant association with blood pressure control, eye examinations, or LDL cholesterol control. Racial, ethnic and gender disparities in blood sugar control persisted even among people who were insured, with Hispanic/Latino and African American patients having worse outcomes.
studies.why_it_matters: Coverage alone does not guarantee that the eye exams, cholesterol checks and blood pressure control that prevent blindness, amputation and heart attacks actually happen — patients and families may need to track these themselves.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have type 2 diabetes, don't assume being insured means your care is complete: ask specifically when your last dilated eye exam, cholesterol panel and blood pressure review happened, and request them by name if they've lapsed.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and senior living health coordinators: consider keeping a simple checklist of the four core diabetes care measures for each resident, since this analysis shows coverage status alone predicts only whether an HbA1c got drawn — not whether the rest of the preventive package was delivered.
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of only 12 observational studies rated moderate quality with moderate risk of bias; high heterogeneity across outcomes; cannot establish causation; studies covered adults with type 2 diabetes generally, not an older-adult-specific population; single-author review.

studies.title: Hospital-level care delivered at home worked as well as a hospital bed — and patients liked it better
studies.the_study: Researchers in Taiwan ran a prospective non-randomized pilot trial comparing hospital-at-home care with standard inpatient admission for 144 homebound older adults with acute infections needing hospital-level treatment (83 treated at home, 61 in hospital) across 5 hospitals and 13 community clinics. Most patients were frail, chronically ill and functionally dependent. Recovery rates (86.7% at home vs 95.1% in hospital) and deaths during treatment (2.4% vs 3.3%) did not differ significantly, about 11% of home patients needed transfer to hospital, and the home group had a shorter treatment episode (9.72 vs 11.85 days) plus significantly higher satisfaction and willingness to choose the model again.
studies.why_it_matters: For frail older adults, a hospital admission often brings delirium, deconditioning and infection risk; this is early evidence that intravenous antibiotics, point-of-care testing and remote monitoring can be delivered safely at home without the trade-offs families fear.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are homebound and chronically ill, it's worth asking your doctor or home-care team whether your area offers a hospital-at-home program and what would happen if you got worse overnight — these programs are expanding, and this trial suggests patients who used one would choose it again.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For home-care agencies and senior living operators, the findings sketch out what the staffing model actually requires — interprofessional visits, IV therapy, point-of-care diagnostics and remote monitoring — and the roughly 1-in-10 escalation rate sets a realistic expectation for how often a hospital transfer plan will be needed.
studies.caveats: Non-randomized design, so patients were not comparably assigned and selection bias is likely; pilot scale (N=144); conducted entirely within Taiwan's integrated home-based medical care system, which may not generalize to other countries; satisfaction outcomes self-reported; short follow-up (30 days).

studies.title: Older adults on statins got the same benefit from hospital exercise — maybe more — with no muscle problems
studies.the_study: Researchers reanalyzed a randomized trial of 310 acutely hospitalized patients over age 75 (average age 87, 58.7% women) who received either a supervised multicomponent exercise program or usual care, asking whether taking statins changed how much patients benefited. Exercise improved function regardless of statin use, and in exploratory models statin users actually gained slightly more on the Barthel Index of daily function (5.58 points, 95% CI 0.44–10.7). No statin-related muscle problems occurred during the exercise program.
studies.why_it_matters: Muscle aches are the most common reason older adults stop statins, and worry about exercising on them can discourage activity during a hospital stay — this analysis suggests that concern did not materialize in a very old, acutely ill group.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you take a statin and are admitted to the hospital, that's not a reason to skip the ward's exercise or mobility program — ask whether supervised walking and strength work are available, and don't stop a statin on your own because you're worried about exercise.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For rehab and nursing staff, the result argues against reflexively deprescribing statins in acutely ill very old patients on the grounds that they'll interfere with mobilization — though the apparent extra benefit for statin users should be treated as a hypothesis, not a reason to prescribe.
studies.caveats: Secondary, exploratory analysis of a trial not designed to test this question; observational comparison of statin users vs non-users within the trial (cannot establish causation); single health system in Spain; population was very old and acutely hospitalized, so results may not generalize to healthier community-dwelling older adults.

studies.title: VR headsets made Tai Chi lessons more fun for older adults — but no more effective than a video
studies.the_study: Researchers randomized 106 community-dwelling older adults in China to learn Tai Chi movements either through an immersive VR headset or through content-matched 2D video instruction, with 92 completing the full analysis. On the primary outcome — a knowledge test of movement sequences — the two groups were statistically indistinguishable. VR scored better on experience measures (competence, flow, lower tension), and cybersickness was rare: 78% of VR participants reported zero symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: As senior living communities invest in virtual reality equipment, this is a useful reality check: the headset may make an activity more engaging, but it did not teach movement better than an ordinary screen in this head-to-head test.
studies.story_angle_primary: If a VR exercise class is offered where you live, it's reasonable to try it — most participants had no dizziness or nausea and found it absorbing — but don't assume the headset will teach you Tai Chi any faster than following along with a video.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For activity directors and purchasing managers, this strengthens the case for evaluating VR on engagement and participation rather than learning outcomes, and for budgeting around technical exclusions and dropouts (14 of 106 participants lacked complete data).
studies.caveats: Short-term, single-session design with no follow-up; the outcome was movement knowledge, not actual motor performance; participants were community-dwelling volunteers in China who may not represent frailer or less tech-willing older adults; experience outcomes self-reported.

studies.title: Autistic adults over 50 report far more memory and thinking problems than tests can detect
studies.the_study: In the first systematic review and meta-analysis on the topic, researchers pooled 15 cross-sectional studies comparing objective and subjective cognition in autistic adults aged 50 and over (or those with high autistic traits) with neurotypical peers. Autistic participants reported substantially greater subjective cognitive difficulty (d = 0.90) — a large difference — yet objective testing showed only small gaps in processing speed, verbal fluency and working memory, and no differences in other domains.
studies.why_it_matters: With a generation of undiagnosed and late-diagnosed autistic adults now reaching later life, this suggests cognitive aging is broadly similar to neurotypical peers, but self-reported complaints may be driven by something other than measurable decline — and risk being either dismissed or misread as early dementia.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're an autistic older adult and feel your thinking has slipped, this review suggests those feelings are real and common but may not show up on standard tests — worth raising with a clinician who understands autism in later life rather than assuming it means dementia.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and care staff, the gap between reported and measured cognition is a flag to look for other explanations — fatigue, sensory load, anxiety, increased demands on masking — before concluding that a self-reported memory complaint signals neurodegeneration.
studies.caveats: All included studies were cross-sectional with no longitudinal data, so actual rates of decline over time are unknown; participants over 65 were underrepresented; high heterogeneity across analyses; many samples were defined by autistic traits rather than formal diagnosis; subjective outcomes are self-reported by design.

studies.title: For people with dementia living at home, starting cognition — not age — predicts how fast daily skills slip away
studies.the_study: Danish researchers screened nearly 7,000 records and pooled 13 longitudinal studies covering 9,490 community-dwelling adults aged 65+ with dementia to identify what predicts decline in activities of daily living. Only baseline cognitive score (MMSE), age, sex, education and living alone had been studied consistently enough to pool. Better baseline cognition predicted slower functional decline, while age and years of education showed no significant effect; evidence on sex and living alone was very weak.
studies.why_it_matters: Families constantly ask how quickly a relative with dementia will lose the ability to dress, cook or manage money — this says chronological age is not the answer, and that current cognitive testing is the most reliable, if still modest, guide available.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a partner has been diagnosed with dementia, don't let age alone shape your expectations about how long independence will last — ask what your current cognitive testing suggests, and use that to time decisions about home modifications and support.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care planners and home-care services, the review is a warning that the prognostic evidence base is thin and mostly at high risk of bias; baseline cognition is the one defensible planning anchor, and confident predictions based on age or living situation are not supported.
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of observational studies (cannot establish causation); risk of bias was high for selection in 16 of 19 reports and attrition in 14; effect sizes were small (SMD -0.05 for cognition); most candidate predictors could not be pooled at all; evidence certainty was only moderate at best.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**

- **Products sold for brain health keep outrunning the human evidence.** Last week's *40 Hz light and sound therapy for Alzheimer's: promising brain scans, but no proven memory benefit yet* (PMID 42828668) and *The supplement NAC is being studied for Parkinson's — but the human evidence is thinner than the headlines suggest* (PMID 40988585) now have a starker companion: *Vitamin E for brain blood flow: decades of research, and not a single human trial* (PMID 41964896), where a six-database search turned up zero clinical studies. *Adding a second drug to donepezil hasn't yet been proven better than donepezil alone for Alzheimer's* (PMID 42816922) extends the same caution to prescription practice rather than retail shelves.
- **Technology raises engagement without changing the outcome it is sold on.** *Older adults learned to use a digital memory aid on their own — a coach added nothing* (PMID 42043435) and *Exergaming didn't beat doing nothing for thinking skills in Parkinson's — but anxiety dropped and stayed down* (PMID 42576230) are joined by *VR headsets made Tai Chi lessons more fun for older adults — but no more effective than a video* (PMID 42814913): better experience scores, identical learning.
- **A clean functional score can hide real impairment.** Last week's *How fast you walk in the clinic isn't how fast you walk at home* (PMID 42296946) and *Uneven test scores — not just low ones — may be an early warning sign of dementia* (PMID 40847579) are echoed by *One in three cerebral stroke-clot survivors has lasting cognitive problems — even those who look fully recovered* (PMID 41416684), where 28.6% of people rated as having no disability still had measurable cognitive impairment, and by *Autistic adults over 50 report far more memory and thinking problems than tests can detect* (PMID 42815817), which runs the same mismatch in the opposite direction.
- **Short, low-intensity movement is the realistic exercise target in later life.** *"Exercise snacks" boost fitness in younger adults — but the payoff looks different after 50* (PMID 42571752) is reinforced by *A step-counter and a simple self-monitoring routine broke up long sitting spells in older day-care clients with heart conditions* (PMID 42830457), where the gains showed up in light activity and fewer 30-minute sitting spells rather than in vigorous effort.
- **Sleep keeps surfacing as a clinical variable, not a comfort issue.** Following *Poor sleep plus inflammation: a double hit to the brain's internal GPS in older adults* (PMID 42264275) and *Too little sleep — or too much — linked to higher risk of chronic lung disease in a 9-year study* (PMID 42246285), this week adds the caregiver side: *Behavioral sleep programs help dementia caregivers rest — but the evidence is thinner than it looks* (PMID 42472449).
- **Where care is delivered is becoming an older-adult story in its own right.** *When an urban hospital closes, older and uninsured residents bear the brunt* (PMID 42343058) is answered this week by *Hospital-level care delivered at home worked as well as a hospital bed — and patients liked it better* (PMID 42816724) and complicated by *Insurance gets you the blood test — but it doesn't close the diabetes care gap* (PMID 42380557).

**Advances**

- **Family caregiving moves from "burden" to "expectations."** Last week's *For many minority caregivers, caring for a parent with dementia is about preserving culture — not just managing illness* (PMID 41781013) argued that services misread what families want; *When grown children fall short of expectations, older parents pay a mental health price* (PMID 42029190) supplies the parent's side of that same ledger, finding relationship quality mattered more than how close children lived.
- **Prognosis after a dementia diagnosis gets a defensible anchor.** Where last week's imaging and variability reviews asked what predicts who will decline, *For people with dementia living at home, starting cognition — not age — predicts how fast daily skills slip away* (PMID 42814268) narrows the answer for families already past diagnosis — and warns that the rest of the prognostic evidence base is thin.

**Counterpoints**

- **More medication is not more protection.** Last week's theme that the expensive added ingredient could often be dropped (PMID 42043435) now reaches drug regimens: *Adding a second drug to donepezil hasn't yet been proven better than donepezil alone for Alzheimer's* (PMID 42816922) found no combination beat donepezil by itself on any outcome.
- **Statins and mobilization are not in conflict.** Against the common instinct to deprescribe or go easy, *Older adults on statins got the same benefit from hospital exercise — maybe more — with no muscle problems* (PMID 42814267) found no statin-related muscle trouble in acutely hospitalized patients averaging 87 years old.

**New themes**

- **Loneliness as several distinct conditions, not one:** *Volunteering and video calls ease loneliness in older adults — scrolling social media does the opposite* (PMID 41934642), *Not all loneliness is the same — and the existential kind hits older adults hardest* (PMID 42590895), and *Phone calls and visits from adult children eased depression in older Icelanders over five years* (PMID 41201818).
- **Autistic aging as a recognized clinical population:** *Autistic adults over 50 report far more memory and thinking problems than tests can detect* (PMID 42815817).
- **Coverage versus care quality:** *Insurance gets you the blood test — but it doesn't close the diabetes care gap* (PMID 42380557).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies this week take apart the standard prescription for lonely older adults — see more people, join more things — and find it mostly doesn't hold. *Volunteering and video calls ease loneliness in older adults — scrolling social media does the opposite* (PMID 41934642) found volunteering, working and newly started video calls predicted less loneliness two years later while in-person visits, outings, club meetings and religious services showed no measurable benefit; *Not all loneliness is the same — and the existential kind hits older adults hardest* (PMID 42590895) found the form least touched by company was the one most strongly tied to depression and anxiety; and *Phone calls and visits from adult children eased depression in older Icelanders over five years* (PMID 41201818) and *When grown children fall short of expectations, older parents pay a mental health price* (PMID 42029190) both point to the particular, repeated contact of close family — and its emotional quality — rather than social volume.

**Why pitch this now:** Loneliness programming has become a standard offering in senior living communities, health plans and local aging agencies, and nearly all of it is built on the assumption that more activities and more visits are the cure — an assumption that this batch, taken together, does not support.

**Angle:** A piece for older adults and adult children on what actually seems to shift loneliness — purpose, a standing phone call, honest conversation about what is missing — and how to tell which kind of lonely you or your parent are, with a sidebar for activity directors on auditing a calendar that may be measuring attendance instead of connection.

**Potential headlines:**
- Volunteering and a Standing Phone Call Helped. Group Outings Didn't.
- A Full Activity Calendar May Not Touch the Loneliness That Hurts Most
- When You Are Surrounded by People and Still Feel Alone

**Potential outlets:**
- **Next Avenue** — written for adult children who call dutifully and wonder whether it helps; these studies give them a concrete answer about which contact mattered.
- **Caring.com** — families comparing communities often judge them by the activity calendar, and this reframes what that calendar can and cannot deliver.
- **LeadingAge** — directly challenges how nonprofit providers program and staff for social connection, including the case for building real volunteer roles for residents.
- **Generations Journal** — the existential-loneliness finding is a practice-and-training argument for clinicians and social services, well suited to adapted research rather than straight news.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Behavioral sleep programs help dementia caregivers rest — but the evidence is thinner than it looks (PMID 42472449):** What to ask your Area Agency on Aging or Alzheimer's Association chapter about sleep-focused caregiver programs before reaching for a sleeping pill, for a caregiver-advice column.
- **Volunteering and video calls ease loneliness in older adults — scrolling social media does the opposite (PMID 41934642):** Swap some scrolling for a volunteer shift or a standing video call — and an activity-director brief on auditing a calendar full of outings that showed no loneliness benefit, for a consumer aging-well column plus a senior-living trade brief.
- **Not all loneliness is the same — and the existential kind hits older adults hardest (PMID 42590895):** Naming existential loneliness for people who have plenty of company and still feel apart, and why conversations about meaning and loss belong in late-life care, for a consumer mental-health explainer.
- **When grown children fall short of expectations, older parents pay a mental health price (PMID 42029190):** Moving a parent closer may not help if the support feels obligatory — ask what they actually expected, for a caregiver-advice column or family-relationships feature.
- **Phone calls and visits from adult children eased depression in older Icelanders over five years (PMID 41201818):** The case for scheduling rather than spontaneity, including a cue for staff to notice when a resident's calls and visits go quiet, for a consumer piece on family routines and a senior-living clinical brief.
- **A step-counter and a simple self-monitoring routine broke up long sitting spells in older day-care clients with heart conditions (PMID 42830457):** If exercise classes are out of reach, the target is interrupting long sits — ask a day program or physical therapist for a device and a daily number, for a consumer fitness explainer and a day-center operations brief.
- **Adding a second drug to donepezil hasn't yet been proven better than donepezil alone for Alzheimer's (PMID 42816922):** Three questions to ask when a second Alzheimer's medication is proposed — what benefit, measured how, and when would we stop, for a consumer health explainer or medication-review trade brief.
- **One in three cerebral stroke-clot survivors has lasting cognitive problems — even those who look fully recovered (PMID 41416684):** "No disability" on discharge paperwork is not the end of the conversation — push for cognitive screening in follow-up visits, for a caregiver-advice column or local-news health segment.
- **Vitamin E for brain blood flow: decades of research, and not a single human trial (PMID 41964896):** A plain-language reality check on a supplement bought for brain health, plus why it belongs on your pharmacist's list if you take aspirin or a blood thinner, for a consumer health or consumer-protection column.
- **Insurance gets you the blood test — but it doesn't close the diabetes care gap (PMID 42380557):** A four-item checklist — HbA1c, dilated eye exam, cholesterol, blood pressure — to request by name, for a consumer chronic-disease explainer and a senior-living health-coordinator brief.
- **Hospital-level care delivered at home worked as well as a hospital bed — and patients liked it better (PMID 42816724):** What to ask about a hospital-at-home program, starting with what happens if you get worse overnight, alongside the roughly 1-in-10 escalation rate operators should plan for, for a consumer explainer and a home-care trade brief.
- **Older adults on statins got the same benefit from hospital exercise — maybe more — with no muscle problems (PMID 42814267):** Being on a statin is not a reason to skip the ward's mobility program, and not a reason to stop the drug on your own, for a consumer medication explainer and a rehab-staff brief.
- **VR headsets made Tai Chi lessons more fun for older adults — but no more effective than a video (PMID 42814913):** Evaluate VR purchases on engagement and participation, not learning claims — and budget for the residents who drop out or can't use the equipment, for a senior-living technology trade brief.
- **Autistic adults over 50 report far more memory and thinking problems than tests can detect (PMID 42815817):** A late-diagnosed generation is reaching later life, and reported memory trouble that doesn't show on tests may point to fatigue, sensory load or anxiety rather than dementia, for a consumer health explainer or clinician-facing trade piece.
- **For people with dementia living at home, starting cognition — not age — predicts how fast daily skills slip away (PMID 42814268):** Don't let a birthday set expectations for how long independence lasts — use current cognitive testing to time home modifications and support, for a caregiver-planning column and a home-care trade brief.

# Fact-Check Report: Senior Living Research Digest — New This Week — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-05 | **Studies reviewed:** 15
**Primary audience:** older adults and seniors | **Secondary audience:** families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

---

### Study 1: Behavioral sleep programs help dementia caregivers rest — but the evidence is thinner than it looks
**PMID:** 42472449 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 2: Volunteering and video calls ease loneliness in older adults — scrolling social media does the opposite
**PMID:** 41934642 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Cross-sectional finding presented as longitudinal** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "older adults who kept volunteering, who worked, and who newly took up video calls with family reported less loneliness two years later, while time spent on social networking sites went the other way"
- **Abstract says:** "Work and volunteering were cross-sectionally associated with lower loneliness at T1, whereas social network site visits were associated with higher loneliness. Continued volunteering over two years and newly initiated video calls with family/friends were associated with lower loneliness at T2"
- **Problem:** Only continued volunteering and newly initiated video calls were associated with loneliness two years later. Work and social-network-site use were cross-sectional (baseline) associations only, so attaching them to the 'two years later' result overstates the longitudinal evidence.
- **Suggested fix:** "Separate the two: 'at baseline, working and volunteering went with less loneliness and social media use with more; over two years, only continued volunteering and newly started video calls predicted lower loneliness.'"

**Issue B. Causal verb in headline for observational data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Volunteering and video calls ease loneliness in older adults — scrolling social media does the opposite"
- **Abstract says:** "Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Associations … were associated with lower loneliness at T2, controlling for T1 loneliness and other covariates."
- **Problem:** 'Ease' and 'does the opposite' assert causation from a regression analysis of observational survey waves; the digest's own caveats note reverse causation is plausible.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to 'linked to less loneliness' / 'tracked with more loneliness'."

### Study 3: Not all loneliness is the same — and the existential kind hits older adults hardest
**PMID:** 42590895 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 4: When grown children fall short of expectations, older parents pay a mental health price
**PMID:** 42029190 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Advice not supported by the review** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "naming expectations out loud, rather than waiting for them to be met, is where researchers see the relationship quality that protects mood"
- **Abstract says:** "Relational reciprocity and emotionally meaningful intergenerational bonds are of utmost importance."
- **Problem:** The review reports that relationship quality matters more than proximity; it does not test or recommend explicitly voicing expectations, so this is presented as a research finding when it is the digest's own inference.
- **Suggested fix:** "Attribute the suggestion to the digest rather than the researchers, e.g. 'the review points to relational warmth and reciprocity, not distance, as what matters most.'"

**Issue B. Causal headline for a narrative review** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "When grown children fall short of expectations, older parents pay a mental health price"
- **Abstract says:** "Filial discrepancies and their psychological interpretations appear to be associated with depressive symptoms and loneliness among older adults."
- **Problem:** 'Pay a mental health price' reads as cause and effect from a review of heterogeneous observational studies that the authors describe only in associational terms.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to 'is linked to more depression and loneliness in older parents.'"

### Study 5: Phone calls and visits from adult children eased depression in older Icelanders over five years
**PMID:** 41201818 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Mean ages misattributed** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "5,764 community-dwelling older adults at baseline (2002–2006) and 3,316 at follow-up (2007–2011), with mean ages of 77 and 78"
- **Abstract says:** "Among low depressive symptoms (mean age 77) … Among high depressive symptoms (mean age 78)"
- **Problem:** The two mean ages describe the low- and high-depressive-symptom subgroups, not the baseline and follow-up waves.
- **Suggested fix:** "State that the low-symptom group had a mean age of 77 and the high-symptom group 78."

**Issue B. Causal verb in headline** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Phone calls and visits from adult children eased depression in older Icelanders over five years"
- **Abstract says:** "Longitudinal linear regression assessed associations between social questions and GDS score at follow-up … decrease in depressive symptoms was when telephoning children (β: -4.679, p = .002)"
- **Problem:** 'Eased depression' asserts causation from an observational cohort; the digest's caveats concede reverse causation is plausible.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use 'were linked to lower depression scores' in the headline."

**Issue C. Equivalence claim overstated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "while for those doing well, friendships matter just as much as family"
- **Abstract says:** "meeting with children (β: -0.439, p = .007); friends (β: -0.288, p = .002); feeling close to family (β: -0.232, p ≤ .001) and friends (β: -0.217, p = .009)"
- **Problem:** Both family and friend contacts were significant, but the coefficients for children/family were larger; the study did not test whether the two were statistically equivalent.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say 'contact with friends mattered too, alongside family' rather than 'just as much.'"

**Issue D. Regression coefficient described as a point drop** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "telephone contact with children was associated with a GDS drop of nearly five points"
- **Abstract says:** "decrease in depressive symptoms was when telephoning children (β: -4.679, p = .002)"
- **Problem:** β = -4.679 is a regression coefficient whose scaling (per unit of the contact variable) is not described in the abstract; presenting it as a straightforward five-point GDS fall may overstate the magnitude for readers.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that this is a regression coefficient of -4.7 GDS points per unit of telephone contact, with the units unspecified in the abstract."

### Study 6: A step-counter and a simple self-monitoring routine broke up long sitting spells in older day-care clients with heart conditions
**PMID:** 42830457 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 7: Adding a second drug to donepezil hasn't yet been proven better than donepezil alone for Alzheimer's
**PMID:** 42816922 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 8: One in three cerebral stroke-clot survivors has lasting cognitive problems — even those who look fully recovered
**PMID:** 41416684 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Prevalence stated at the upper bound** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "One in three cerebral stroke-clot survivors has lasting cognitive problems"
- **Abstract says:** "Cognitive impairment affects roughly one-fifth to one-third of CVT survivors (19-29%)"
- **Problem:** The pooled estimate is a range from 19.25% (low-risk-of-bias studies) to 29.20% (overall analysis); stating 'one in three' presents the highest figure as the finding and rounds 29% up.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use 'one in five to one in three' or 'about a quarter to a third' in the headline and the 'Why it matters' line."

### Study 9: Vitamin E for brain blood flow: decades of research, and not a single human trial
**PMID:** 41964896 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Absolute 'never conducted' claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "with no human trial ever conducted"
- **Abstract says:** "Six databases … were searched in 2024 … Of the 335 records returned, no clinical studies were identified."
- **Problem:** The review found no clinical studies meeting its inclusion criteria in a 2024 search of six databases; that is not the same as no human trial ever having been conducted on vitamin E and cerebrovascular function.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write 'the review found no human clinical studies meeting its criteria.'"

**Issue B. Safety advice drawn from animal data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "because vitamin E affects platelet clumping, it's worth telling your doctor or pharmacist you take it, especially if you're also on a blood thinner or aspirin"
- **Abstract says:** "studies examining platelet aggregation reported delayed thrombus formation, likely mediated by reduced oxidative stress and improved endothelial function"
- **Problem:** The platelet-aggregation finding in this review comes from preclinical animal studies; the digest presents it as an established human pharmacological effect underpinning a clinical caution.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that the platelet effect was observed in animal models and that interaction concerns come from broader clinical guidance, not this review."

### Study 10: Insurance gets you the blood test — but it doesn't close the diabetes care gap
**PMID:** 42380557 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Gender disparity attributed to the wrong outcome** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Racial, ethnic and gender disparities in blood sugar control persisted even among people who were insured"
- **Abstract says:** "Racial and ethnic disparities in glycemic control persisted among insured individuals … and gender disparities were also observed, particularly in lipid control."
- **Problem:** The abstract locates the persisting glycemic-control disparities in race and ethnicity; gender disparities were observed particularly in lipid control, not blood sugar control.
- **Suggested fix:** "Split the sentence: racial and ethnic disparities persisted in blood sugar control, while gender disparities showed up particularly in lipid control."

### Study 11: Hospital-level care delivered at home worked as well as a hospital bed — and patients liked it better
**PMID:** 42816724 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Equivalence claimed from a non-significant pilot result** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Hospital-level care delivered at home worked as well as a hospital bed — and patients liked it better"
- **Abstract says:** "Remission/complete treatment was achieved in most patients in both groups (86.7% vs. 95.1%; p = 0.153)... This pilot trial... provides preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility and acceptability of community-initiated hospital-level acute care at home (ACAH) for frail older adults."
- **Problem:** A non-significant difference in a small, non-randomized pilot (recovery 8.4 percentage points lower at home) is not evidence of equivalence; the authors claim only feasibility and acceptability, not comparable effectiveness.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to something like "Hospital-level care at home looked feasible and was preferred by patients — but this pilot was too small to prove it matches a hospital bed.""

**Issue B. Safety overstated in "Why it matters"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this is early evidence that intravenous antibiotics, point-of-care testing and remote monitoring can be delivered safely at home without the trade-offs families fear"
- **Abstract says:** "The HaH group received interprofessional visits, intravenous pharmacotherapy, point-of-care diagnostics, and remote patient monitoring... Mortality during the treatment episode was low (2.4% vs. 3.3%; p = 1.000). Nine HaH patients (10.8%) required clinical escalation."
- **Problem:** "Without the trade-offs families fear" goes beyond a pilot that was not powered for safety outcomes; the abstract also says "intravenous pharmacotherapy," not specifically antibiotics.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "early, preliminary evidence that IV therapy, point-of-care testing and remote monitoring can be delivered at home, with escalation to hospital needed in about 1 in 10 cases.""

### Study 12: Older adults on statins got the same benefit from hospital exercise — maybe more — with no muscle problems
**PMID:** 42814267 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 13: VR headsets made Tai Chi lessons more fun for older adults — but no more effective than a video
**PMID:** 42814913 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 14: Autistic adults over 50 report far more memory and thinking problems than tests can detect
**PMID:** 42815817 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 15: For people with dementia living at home, starting cognition — not age — predicts how fast daily skills slip away
**PMID:** 42814268 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Behavioral sleep programs help dementia caregivers rest — but the evidence is thinner than it looks | ✅ Accurate | All numbers (21 RCTs, 1,964 caregivers, mean age 64, ~75% female, 5 trials/334 participants, MD -1.27 PSQI points), the risk-of-bias and very-low-certainty ratings, and the citation details match the abstract. Framing appropriately hedged. |
| 2 | Volunteering and video calls ease loneliness in older adults — scrolling social media does the opposite | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample sizes, mean ages and the pattern of significant/non-significant associations are correct, but the senior-facing angle folds work (a cross-sectional T1 finding) into the two-year longitudinal result, and the headline uses causal verbs for observational data. |
| 3 | Not all loneliness is the same — and the existential kind hits older adults hardest | ✅ Accurate | N=237, mean age 70.87 (rounded to 70.9), the three loneliness types, all three linked to depression with existential strongest, and existential as the only type tied to anxiety all match. Cross-sectional nature and single-country limitation are flagged in Caveats. |
| 4 | When grown children fall short of expectations, older parents pay a mental health price | ⚠️ Minor issues | Search window (2011-2025), six databases, JBI appraisal, the depression/loneliness association and the 'relationship quality outweighs proximity' finding all match. One story-angle claim goes beyond what the abstract reports. |
| 5 | Phone calls and visits from adult children eased depression in older Icelanders over five years | ⚠️ Minor issues | Cohort, wave sizes, dates, seven social questions and the key coefficients are reported correctly, but the mean ages are misattributed to the waves rather than the depression subgroups, the headline is causal, and 'friendships matter just as much as family' overstates the comparison. |
| 6 | A step-counter and a simple self-monitoring routine broke up long sitting spells in older day-care clients with heart conditions | ✅ Accurate | Parent trial N=52, 36 eligible with cardiovascular conditions, 33 analyzed (19/14), the significant group×time interactions and the null results for MVPA and EQ-5D-5L all match. Exploratory, hypothesis-generating nature is flagged in Caveats as the authors describe it. |
| 7 | Adding a second drug to donepezil hasn't yet been proven better than donepezil alone for Alzheimer's | ✅ Accurate | 41 trials, 9,822 patients, masitinib ranking highest by SUCRA, significance versus placebo but not versus donepezil monotherapy, and 'mostly moderate to low' certainty all match. Framing appropriately restrained for a network meta-analysis. |
| 8 | One in three cerebral stroke-clot survivors has lasting cognitive problems — even those who look fully recovered | ⚠️ Minor issues | Study counts (11 observational + 1 RCT, 801 patients), the 19-29% range, domain-specific prevalences and the 28.6% figure for mRS 0 are all correct; the headline and 'Why it matters' pick the top of the range. |
| 9 | Vitamin E for brain blood flow: decades of research, and not a single human trial | ⚠️ Minor issues | Six databases, 335 records, zero clinical studies, 10 preclinical studies and the animal findings are reported correctly; one absolute claim goes slightly beyond what a 2024 database search can establish, and the platelet advice rests on preclinical data. |
| 10 | Insurance gets you the blood test — but it doesn't close the diabetes care gap | ⚠️ Minor issues | 12 studies, 2000-2025, the significant HbA1c testing association, the three null outcomes, moderate quality/risk of bias and single authorship are all accurate; gender disparities are slightly mislocated. |
| 11 | Hospital-level care delivered at home worked as well as a hospital bed — and patients liked it better | ⚠️ Minor issues | Numbers, design and setting all match the abstract; the headline and "Why it matters" read an underpowered null result as proof of equivalence and safety. |
| 12 | Older adults on statins got the same benefit from hospital exercise — maybe more — with no muscle problems | ✅ Accurate | Sample size, age, sex split, Barthel Index effect (5.58 points, 95% CI 0.44–10.7) and absence of muscle adverse events all match; exploratory nature is clearly flagged. |
| 13 | VR headsets made Tai Chi lessons more fun for older adults — but no more effective than a video | ✅ Accurate | Randomization (106, 92 analyzed), null primary outcome, favorable game-experience findings and 78% zero-symptom cybersickness figure all match the abstract. |
| 14 | Autistic adults over 50 report far more memory and thinking problems than tests can detect | ✅ Accurate | Fifteen cross-sectional studies, d = 0.90 for subjective difficulty, small objective gaps in processing speed/verbal fluency/working memory, and the stated limitations (no longitudinal data, under-65 skew, heterogeneity, trait-defined samples) all match. |
| 15 | For people with dementia living at home, starting cognition — not age — predicts how fast daily skills slip away | ✅ Accurate | Records screened (6,915), 13 studies/9,490 participants, poolable predictors, direction of findings, risk-of-bias counts (16/19 selection, 14/19 attrition) and SMD -0.05 are all reproduced correctly, and the tiny effect size is flagged in Caveats. |

**Total issues:** 14 (12 Minor, 2 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 7
**Entries cleared:** 8
